title: Ferritin: Optimal Levels, Reference Ranges & Functional Medicine Interpretation | The Lamkin Clinic | Lamkin Clinic
abstract:
## 1. What This Test Measures  
Ferritin is the body's primary iron storage protein, a large spherical protein shell that stores and releases iron as needed by cells throughout the body. Serum ferritin measures the concentration of this protein circulating in the bloodstream, and serves as the most reliable proxy for total body iron stores available on a routine blood test.  
Every cell in the body requires iron for fundamental functions: mitochondrial energy production via the electron transport chain, oxygen transport in red blood cells, DNA synthesis, thyroid hormone metabolism, and neurotransmitter production. When iron stores fall, these processes are progressively impaired, often producing significant symptoms well before hemoglobin drops low enough to qualify as anemia on a conventional lab report.  
Ferritin has a critical dual clinical role that makes it uniquely complex to interpret:  
- **When low:**ferritin directly reflects depleted iron stores, a state of functional iron deficiency even when serum iron or hemoglobin may still appear normal.
- **When high:**ferritin can reflect either true iron overload OR an acute-phase inflammatory response. Ferritin rises non-specifically with infection, inflammation, liver disease, metabolic syndrome, and malignancy, completely independent of iron status.
## 7. How to Improve This Marker  
For Low Ferritin  
- Increase heme iron sources: red meat (grass-fed beef, lamb), dark poultry meat, organ meats (liver is the richest source)
- Pair non-heme iron foods (spinach, lentils, tofu) with vitamin C to enhance absorption
- Avoid tea, coffee, and calcium-rich foods within 1 to 2 hours of iron-rich meals; they inhibit absorption
- Cook in cast iron cookware; transfers small amounts of dietary iron
- Address heavy menstrual bleeding with appropriate gynecological evaluation
- Test and treat H. pylori or celiac disease if present
- Optimize stomach acid production; consider betaine HCl if hypochlorhydric  
Supplementation  
- **Iron bisglycinate:**most tolerable oral form; significantly less GI side effects than ferrous sulfate; 25 to 50mg elemental iron daily
- **Ferrous sulfate:**standard, highly effective, lower cost; take with vitamin C; GI side effects common
- **Liquid iron formulations:**useful when tablet absorption is problematic
- **IV iron infusion:**for severe deficiency, malabsorption, or when oral iron is not tolerated; most rapid repletion method
- Take iron on alternate days; research shows every-other-day dosing achieves similar repletion with better absorption and fewer side effects
- Retest ferritin at 3 to 4 months to assess repletion progress  
For High Ferritin  
- First step: check iron saturation (TSAT); above 45% strongly suggests true iron overload; below 45% with high ferritin suggests inflammatory elevation
## 9. When Testing Is Recommended  
- Any woman with fatigue, hair loss, brain fog, or poor exercise tolerance regardless of hemoglobin level
- Premenopausal women with heavy menstrual periods
- Vegetarians and vegans; significantly increased risk of iron deficiency
- Athletes, particularly female endurance athletes (high demand and foot-strike hemolysis)
- Restless legs syndrome; ferritin evaluation is a standard first step
- Individuals with GI symptoms or known malabsorption: celiac, Crohn's, GERD on PPIs
- Family history of hemochromatosis; screen with ferritin and TSAT
- Unexplained liver enzyme elevation; ferritin is part of a complete liver assessment
- Annual monitoring in all patients with known iron deficiency until ferritin reaches optimal range
- Patients with metabolic syndrome and elevated ferritin to distinguish inflammatory from iron-overload etiology
